## Choosing the right Microcontroller
I initially chose the XIAO-ESP32-C3 because that's what SharKingStudios Starbie tutorial recommended, but down the line, I started to realize why it was a good fit for the project-its small compact size let me fit all components on one PCB inside starbie's small enclosure, it supports lithium battery charge and discharge management, multiple GPIO pins with different functions needed for the sensors and inputs, and the Arduino IDE supports the ESP32 boards.
![MCU Image](https://cdn.hackclub.com/01a17b20-fec5-7803-9164-a3d58aba7806/Screenshot%202026-10-26%20221039.png)

## "Petting" Sensor
The XIAO ESP32-C3 has no capacitive touch input I could rely on for a petting gesture, so I needed an external component for that. My first choice was the AT42QT1010-TSHR because of its ability to detect near-proximity touch, but I changed my mind because it has a maximum on-time timer, that is, there is a maximum number of consecutive seconds it can detect the touch for, whereas I wanted the starbie to react as long as it's being touched, so I went with the AT42QT1011-TSHR.
![QT1011](https://cdn.hackclub.com/01a17b25-2460-7045-bce3-fc9dba53810d/Screenshot%202026-10-26%20221621.png)

 I used the AT42QT1011-TSHR SOT23-6 datasheet provided by Microchip Technology as my learning source. I added a bypass capacitor between the VDD(pin 5) and VSS(pin 2). This stabilizes the chip's power supply (more like a mini power reservoir), it also reduces electrical noise and helps prevent false touch triggers. Also added a sampling capacitor between the SNSK and SNS, this actually does a major work in detecting the touch because a change in capacitance occurs when the sense electrode is touched (via your body's electrical properties) and then the circuit detects the change in capacitance. A resistor between SNSK and the sense electrode protects against ESD and EMC effects.
![QT1011 datasheet](https://cdn.hackclub.com/01a17b22-f6be-7ead-91f0-80d2990b5097/Screenshot%202026-10-26%20221358.png)
 One mistake I made was adding a real capacitor between the pad and GND because the datasheet draws one, whereas it is the natural capacitance of the copper pad to its surroundings. Adding a real one would only load the electrode and hurt sensitivity, so I deleted it. I wired the out pin to XIAO's D6 pin and that tells the MCU 'hey, I was touched'.
![QT1011 PCB](https://cdn.hackclub.com/01a17b28-7936-7f63-9c91-ac996ef9d7d2/Screenshot%202026-10-26%20221957.png)

## Battery and USB detection
I wanted the starbie to be portable, not just being used when plugged in. The XIAO is capable of using a 3.7V lithum battery, so I settled for the 503450 LiPo battery because of its flat shape, thereby making it easier to sit in the enclosure, and also because it's rechargeable.
![bat image](https://cdn.hackclub.com/01a17b2a-96b8-7825-8b95-ba4bc2c0a5a3/Screenshot%202026-10-26%20222218.png)
I wanted the starbie to react to a low battery level, but the ESP32-C3 does not have pins for that, so I implemented the battery divider approach by msfujino. The battery voltage is divided by 1/2 with 200k resistors and connected to D1(GPIO3).
![bat divider](https://cdn.hackclub.com/01a17b2e-ba18-7d3a-8ff7-cffc7525b300/Screenshot%202026-10-26%20222652.png)
 I initially put the battery divider on D0(GPIO2) but then realized it was a strapping pin, but other ADC pins were occupied, so I moved the DHT11 from D1 to D7 because it didn't require the ADC function and placed the Battery divider on D1. An ADC pin was needed because the battery provides an analog voltage, and the ADC converts the voltage to a digital reading that the firmware can process.
![image II](https://cdn.hackclub.com/01a17b3e-d213-769e-9aad-3681a94fec5a/Screenshot%202026-10-26%20224425.png)

I want the starbie to react(a happy face) when plugged in, giving the illusion of it being fed(a digital pet eats electricity). The USB port supplies 5 volts. The XIAO's 5V pin(VBUS) is connected to that USB 5V supply, which is too high for a GPIO, so I used 2 resistors to bring that down, the midpoint sits near 3 V, which a digital input reads as high, and then connected that to D10
![bat level](https://cdn.hackclub.com/01a17b34-64c6-7bb0-843d-72f02949b527/Screenshot%202026-10-26%20223255.png)

## PCB Layout
At first, I thought footprint meant a sort of mark the components leaves on the PCB, I was so wrong(don't be like me). It's more of assigning the physical layout of a component to its schematic symbol. Several footprints were assigned wrongly (DIP-8, Tag-Connect, a slide-switch footprint, a C6 footprint). I checked the footprint column and reassigned them before laying out anything.
![footprint](https://cdn.hackclub.com/01a17b32-5de2-7ae6-999b-0649ba05d514/Screenshot%202026-10-26%20223039.png)

I drew the star outline like the tutorial's, and also because I wanted it to match its name, 'Starbie'. I placed the XIAO in a way that the USB port extends past the PCB outline. For the sense electrode, I initially used a copper zone, but it kept vanishing. I removed that and built the electrode as a real one-pad SMD footprint.
![pad footprint](https://cdn.hackclub.com/01a17b3a-2d79-7d62-8c29-91f055540f76/Screenshot%202026-10-26%20223921.png)
I considered flipping the pad to the back layer, but kept it on the front because that's simpler and avoids a via. I added a clearance override on the back copper so the ground pour stays away from the area behind the pad.
A major issue I kept facing was routing the wire tracks because tracks were being blocked by other tracks. I changed the position of some components on the PCB, and increased the size of the PCB outline.
I ran the DRC and got many "unconnected" errors for ground pins, which is expected before the pour exists. After the pour, it fixed that and I fixed a stray unconnected via on the sense net.
![PCB](https://cdn.hackclub.com/01a17b3c-5695-7d1e-825e-2c73de22b357/Screenshot%202026-10-26%20224147.png)

## Firmware
I started with the tutorial's starbie.ino file, which already draws the pet, runs the radial menu and reads the DHT11. I added the touch feature by making the pet react when the pin goes from low to high(and add 5 joy points) instead of reacting on every loop while the pin is high. I did it that way because the AT42QT1011 has no time-out, so a hand resting on the pad keeps OUT high, and without the cooldown the pet would throw hearts every frame. I assumed OUT goes high when touched, so I stored it as a constant variable TOUCH_LEVEL, so if the real testing says the opposite, I'd just make a one-line change.
I took 8 readings from the battery divider pin(GPIO3) because taking one reading is almost never accurate or steady, averaging 8 readings brings the output closer to the true value. Then multiplied the result by 2 to undo the two 200k resistors. I added a placeholder threshold of 3400mV for the sad face, might make changes on that upon real testing. I read the battery voltage every 2 seconds.
I first planned to enable USB CDC On Boot, so that the serial monitor would go over the USB-C cable and leave D6 and D7 alone.I then read Seeed's pin-multiplexing page and found that USB serial is already on by default, and D6/D7 only become the UART0 pins if I deliberately open Serial1 on them, which I'm not doing. So I left it as it was, but if Starbie starts acting weird during boot, D6 is my first suspect.
The major thing still left is having the components, so I can test all of this on real hardware.
